In summary, our research is concerned with
the metabolism of dietary essential amino acid methionine in the intestine and its effect on the availability of L-MET to the extraintestinal tissues of piglets.
the effect of dietary L-MET sources (dl-methionine [dl-MET] and dl-2-hydroxymethyl-4-methylhiobutyrate [dl-HMTB]) on the metabolism of methionine in piglets.
the metabolism of DL-MET and its hydroxy analogue, DL-HMTB, in the piglets, which may provide new important information on nutritional efficiency of different AA sources.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the intestinal metabolism of L-MET from DL-MET and its hydroxy analogue, DL-HMTB, in piglets was affected by the distribution of D-AAOX and D-HADH/L-HAOX, and that the similar portal appearance between the two L-MET sources may be due to the relatively higher D-AAOX activity in the intestine than in the stomach, which is responsible for the conversion of DL-HMTB and/or DL-MET to L-MET.
the intestine is a major organ in catabolizing dietary AA to keto-AA, which results in the decrease in extraintestinal availability and efficiency of AA utilization.
the intestine had the highest capacity of D-META utilization to L-META synthesis and its subsequent oxidation to L-META, and the stomach had a substantial capacity of dl-HMTBA utilization to L-MTA.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

DL-HMTB, a more expensive AA source than DL-MET, may be a better choice for the piglet to improve its extraintestinal availability and utilization of L-MET, but this needs further confirmation by using a more sensitive method to determine the portal appearance of L-2-hydroxymethylthiobutanoate (HMTB).
DL-MET is a more suitable L-MET source than DL-HMTB for piglets because it has the advantage of bypassing the extensive catabolic activity of D-AAOX in the intestine.

the intestine and the stomach are the major sites for catabolism and synthesis, respectively, of L-MET in the piglet, and the distribution of enzymes involved in L-MET metabolism is the main factor affecting the availability of L-MET from different sources for protein synthesis in the extraintestinal tissues.

the intestinal catabolism may be reduced by supplying the animal a more stable AA source that is more of which can be metabolized to L-AA and less of which is catabolized to CO(2) and H(2)O in the intestine.
